content: Menorrhagia refers to abnormally heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding. It can also be associated with irregular menstrual cycles. Other terms used to describe this condition include irregular menstruation, heavy or prolonged periods, polymenorrhea, abnormal menstrual periods, and abnormal vaginal bleeding. Overview The menstrual cycle varies among women. On average, menstrual flow occurs every 28 days, with most cycles ranging between 24 and 34 days, and lasts about 4 to 7 days. However, variations in timing and duration can still be considered normal, especially in the first few years after menstruation begins. A small percentage of women may experience cycles shorter than 21 days or longer than 35 days, which may also be normal. Considerations Examples of abnormal bleeding include: Bleeding or spotting between periods. Bleeding after sexual intercourse. Excessively heavy bleeding, such as passing large clots, needing to change protection during the night, or soaking through a pad or tampon every hour for 2-3 consecutive hours. Bleeding lasting more than 7 days or longer than usual. Menstrual cycles occurring less than 28 days apart or more than 35 days apart. Bleeding after menopause. Misinterpreting blood from the rectum or urine as vaginal bleeding. To confirm the source, inserting a tampon can help determine if the bleeding is vaginal. Causes of Menorrhagia Abnormal menstrual bleeding can result from various causes, including: Hormonal imbalances, often referred to as dysfunctional uterine bleeding. Endometrial hyperplasia, which is a thickening of the uterine lining. Uterine cancer. Uterine fibroids or polyps, which are noncancerous growths in the uterine lining, or adenomyosis. Medical conditions such as thyroid or pituitary disorders, diabetes, liver cirrhosis, or systemic lupus erythematosus. Pregnancy complications, such as miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy (implantation of a fertilized egg outside the uterus). Changes in birth control methods, including pills or estrogen use. Use of certain medications, such as steroids or blood thinners (e.g., warfarin or Coumadin). Use of an intrauterine device (IUD) for contraception. Recent trauma, surgery, or uterine procedures. Uterine infections, such as pelvic inflammatory disease. Bleeding disorders, such as Von Willebrand disease. Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Stress, changes in diet or exercise routines, recent weight loss or gain, travel, or illness. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care Contact your doctor if: You soak through a pad or tampon every hour for 2-3 consecutive hours. Your bleeding lasts longer than one week. You are pregnant or suspect you might be pregnant. You experience severe pain, especially if it occurs outside of menstruation. Your periods have been unusually heavy or prolonged for three or more cycles compared to your normal pattern. You have a fever or abnormal vaginal discharge, particularly if it has an odor. You experience bleeding or spotting after menopause. You have bleeding or spotting between periods. You notice symptoms such as nipple discharge, excessive hair growth, a deepening voice, unintentional weight loss or gain, or new acne. Diagnosis Your doctor will perform a physical examination, including a pelvic exam, and ask detailed questions about your symptoms, such as: Your age. Whether your last three menstrual periods were normal in timing and amount. The usual duration of your periods. The number of days between your menstrual cycles. How this cycle and others differ from your usual menstruation. Whether you have passed blood clots. The duration of bleeding during abnormal periods. The heaviness of your bleeding, including the number of pads or tampons used daily. The date of your last menstrual period. Your age at the onset of menstruation. Whether you use birth control pills or an IUD. Whether you take estrogen supplements, aspirin, or anticoagulants like Coumadin or heparin. Whether you have recently given birth, undergone surgery, or experienced trauma near the vagina or uterus. Whether you have had a recent vaginal or uterine infection. Other symptoms, such as abdominal or pelvic pain, nausea, or vomiting. Whether you are pregnant or could be pregnant. Whether you have noticed any growths, lumps, or lesions on the genitals. Whether you have had blood in your stools. Whether you bleed easily. Diagnostic tests may include: Pap smear. Endometrial biopsy. Pelvic ultrasound. Laboratory tests, such as thyroid function tests, complete blood count (CBC), pregnancy test, and serum ferritin levels. Home Care To manage menorrhagia at home: Keep a detailed record of your menstrual cycles and any other bleeding, including: The start and end dates of menstruation. The amount of flow (count the number of pads and tampons used, noting whether they are soaked). Bleeding between periods or after sex. Any other symptoms you experience. Change tampons at least twice a day to prevent infection. Avoid aspirin, as it may prolong bleeding. Ibuprofen is often more effective for relieving menstrual cramps and may reduce blood loss during periods. If you suspect you are pregnant, consult your doctor. Where to Find Medical Care for Menorrhagia Seek medical attention from a healthcare provider or gynecologist for proper evaluation and treatment of menorrhagia.
